SMTO-SSH-0005 — SMTO couldn't tell where the remote computer's trusted key came from

GUID: 4e742e7b-928c-451c-9e73-95cb72515b6f
Slug: ssh-known-hosts-missing
Domain: SSH · Subsystem: ssh

What happened

  • Your SSH command connected, but SSH didn't say which trusted-computers file vouched for the computer. Without that, SMTO can't remember this computer for later commands.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check whether the command already did its job before asking SMTO to run it again. This happens after SSH logs in and the command finishes, so the command most likely already ran.
  2. Ask the person who manages the Gateway computer to add the remote computer's confirmed key to a trusted-computers file, such as ~/.ssh/known_hosts for the Gateway's account. SMTO can only remember computers whose key SSH found in such a file, not ones trusted some other way.
  3. Then ask SMTO to run a harmless SSH command on that computer, such as one that prints the date. A clean connection lets SMTO remember the computer without repeating real work.

What success looks like

  • Later SSH commands to that computer, including ones that need administrator rights, run without this message.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages the Gateway computer. Don't turn off key checking to make the message go away.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The OpenSSH debug log of an initial authenticated connection had no 'Found key in' line naming the known_hosts file and line, so SMTO could not recover the trusted raw host key to pin.

What this means

  • Initial SSH setup lacks the debug-log evidence identifying the known-hosts file and line, despite requiring that source to recover the trusted raw key. Continuity evidence and command outcome are separate. Only the explicit pre-dispatch privilege refusal proves no new execution; observation failure alone cannot prove that a prior SSH command had no effect.

Why this can happen

  • Initial SSH setup lacks the debug-log evidence identifying the known-hosts file and line, despite requiring that source to recover the trusted raw key.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect retained handshake evidence for the known-host source; absence here does not prove no known-hosts file exists.

How to fix it

  • Observation._setup requires the 'debug1: Found key in FILE:LINE' log line to read the trusted raw key on first enrollment. Store the target's verified host key in a known_hosts file OpenSSH reads (UserKnownHostsFile or GlobalKnownHostsFile) instead of supplying it another way such as KnownHostsCommand, then run a harmless ssh command to enroll and confirm the handshake fingerprint matches.
  • Use the supported verified SSH flow with a trusted known-hosts source and inspect its captured identity evidence.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • Supported observation obtains a trusted raw host key and matches the handshake fingerprint.

What not to do

  • Do not automatically disable certificate verification or trust an unverified replacement identity.

Technical notes

  • Continuity evidence and command outcome are separate. Only the explicit pre-dispatch privilege refusal proves no new execution; observation failure alone cannot prove that a prior SSH command had no effect.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
